questions.question: Which fact is usually best represented as a relationship rather than a property?
options: An account's display name
A transfer sent from one account to another at a specific time
A product's description
A customer's preferred locale
questions.explanation: The transfer connects two independently identified entities and has its own meaning and time. Modeling it as a typed relationship makes that path directly queryable.

questions.question: A traversal starts from 1 node, each frontier node has 20 matching relationships, no relationships are pruned, and the maximum depth is 3. How many relationship visits does the simple envelope estimate?
questions.explanation: The traversal inspects 20 relationships at hop 1, 400 at hop 2, and 8,000 at hop 3, for a total of 8,420.

questions.question: Why should a node identity used by MERGE also have a uniqueness constraint?
options: The constraint makes all relationship traversals one hop
The constraint prevents concurrent writers from committing duplicate domain identities
MERGE cannot use parameters without a constraint
The constraint moves the node into JVM heap
questions.explanation: MERGE expresses match-or-create intent, while the uniqueness constraint makes duplicate identities invalid at the database commit boundary.

questions.question: Which query-plan shape is the strongest starting point for a bounded account investigation?
options: Scan every node, then filter the account ID after a variable-length traversal
Seek one constrained Account by ID, then expand typed relationships to a fixed maximum depth
Create a Cartesian product of all accounts and transfers
Sort every relationship before locating the account
questions.explanation: A selective indexed anchor keeps the first cardinality small. Typed relationships, expansion-time predicates, and a maximum depth control frontier growth.

questions.question: What property must a Neo4j driver transaction callback have when transient failures can trigger automatic retries?
options: It must safely produce the same database effect when executed again
It must send external side effects before the database work
It must return an unconsumed result object
It must concatenate parameters into the Cypher string
questions.explanation: A retried callback should be idempotent and should not perform unrecoverable external side effects. Results should be consumed inside the transaction boundary.

questions.question: Which Neo4j memory statement is correct?
options: The page cache stores graph and native index pages, while query and transaction state also need heap and native headroom
JVM heap and page cache are two names for the same allocation
A larger page cache removes the need for durable storage
The operating system needs no memory on a dedicated host
questions.explanation: Neo4j memory has separate consumers. Page cache, heap, native allocations, JVM overhead, plugins, and the operating system must fit one host envelope.

questions.question: In a Neo4j database topology with three primaries, what happens after one primary fails?
options: Writes must stop because every commit requires all three primaries
The two remaining primaries can still form a majority and elect or retain a writer
An asynchronous secondary automatically becomes a voting primary
All committed data must be restored from backup before reads continue
questions.explanation: Two of three primaries form a majority, so the database can preserve write availability after one failure. Another primary failure removes write quorum.

questions.question: A user writes a profile and the next request may read from an asynchronous secondary. What provides read-after-write ordering?
options: A larger driver pool
A causal bookmark passed to the dependent transaction
A backup artifact
A full graph scan
questions.explanation: A bookmark represents the causal position of the write. The dependent read waits for a routed copy to apply at least that position before it executes.
